steps.say: Piles are graded by how far they slip down during straining. Those that stay inside suit a simple office banding, while ones that hang out permanently need a proper operation to remove or lift them.
steps.tx: Internal haemorrhoids grade from **I** (bleeding only) through **II** (prolapse on strain) and **III** (manual return) to **IV** (irreducible prolapse), with grades **I to II** suited to band ligation and grades **III to IV** needing stapled **haemorrhoidopexy** (stapled lifting) or excisional surgery with careful wound care afterwards.

vis.alt: Panels showing internal and external haemorrhoids with a four-grade prolapse scale and banding treatment.
vis.caption: Haemorrhoid grades I to IV with band ligation placed above the painless dentate line. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A tunnel's path decides whether it can simply be laid open. Imaging and a simple bedside rule map the tract against the muscle rings before the surgeon commits to a plan.
steps.tx: **Parks classification** (fistula tract mapping) grades tracts as intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric and extrasphincteric, and the **Goodsall rule** (opening predicts path) expects a curved posterior tract from a midline posterior opening but a straight tract anteriorly in most straightforward cases seen in clinic.

steps.say: Low tunnels through little muscle are simply opened along their length. High tunnels through much muscle must be closed without cutting the ring, using a stitch around the tract or a flap of lining over the inner hole.
steps.tx: Low simple fistulae get **fistulotomy** (laying the tract open), while high tracts involving over **30 percent** (thirty percent) of sphincter need **LIFT** (tying the tract between muscles) or **advancement flap** (lining slid over the hole) to preserve continence and avoid any leakage afterwards.

vis.alt: Cutaway of the anal canal showing internal and external piles with a tunnel crossing the muscle ring.
vis.caption: Transsphincteric fistula crossing the sphincter with internal and external haemorrhoids shown. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A tear that will not heal keeps the muscle in spasm, and relaxing ointments break that cycle for most patients. When six to eight weeks of ointment fail and the classic trio of signs is present, a small cut in the inner muscle cures it.
steps.tx: Chronic posterior fissure with **sentinel pile** (skin tag marker) and hypertrophied papilla failing **6 weeks** (six weeks) of diltiazem or nitrates needs **lateral internal sphincterotomy** (inner muscle release) to the dentate line, curing most cases permanently without harming continence in careful hands.

steps.say: Hairs buried in the natal cleft form pits that repeatedly abscess. Draining settles each flare, but lasting cure moves the scar off the midline where sweat and friction are worst.
steps.tx: Pilonidal pits with abscess get drainage first, then **cleft-lift** (midline flattening) or **Karydakis flap** (side-shifted closure) with **off-midline closure** (scar away from cleft), since midline wounds break down and recur most in the sweaty depths of the cleft where healing is poor.

steps.say: A rectum that telescopes out needs anchoring from above in the young and fit, using a sling of mesh placed through keyholes. The frail elderly are better served by an operation from below under spinal anaesthesia.
steps.tx: Full-thickness prolapse over **5 cm** (five centimetres) in the fit young suits laparoscopic **ventral mesh rectopexy** (front mesh anchoring) sparing nerves, while frail elderly suit perineal Delorme or **Altemeier** (bowel amputation from below) under spinal anaesthesia with rapid recovery and early discharge.

steps.say: Cancer of the anal skin is cured with combined drugs and rays in most cases, without removing the bowel. Surgery that sacrifices continence is kept for the minority whose disease survives full treatment.
steps.tx: Non-metastatic anal squamous carcinoma takes the **Nigro protocol** (combined drug-ray regimen) of 5-fluorouracil with mitomycin plus **chemoradiotherapy** (rays with drugs) first, for tumours under **5 cm** (five centimetres) and larger T3-T4 disease alike, reserving abdominoperineal resection with permanent stoma for salvage in non-responders with persistent disease after full treatment.

steps.say: Boils that keep returning in the groin and buttock folds come from blocked hair follicles, not ordinary infection. Courses of antibiotics calm flares but the tunnels remain, so the diseased skin must come out widely.
steps.tx: **Hidradenitis suppurativa** (blocked hair-follicle disease) of the perineum with recurrent boils and sinus tracts needs **wide excision** (generous skin removal) with healing by secondary intention or flap cover, since antibiotics alone never cure tunnels and established disease returns without surgery.
